graph.title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
graph.abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.
graph.target_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
contributions: A graph-based section scheduler that organizes document generation around a document graph to improve coherence.
An evidence-injection protocol and evidence-aware prompts that attach and verify citations per section.
An audit-friendly, strict JSON output schema and a LaTeX assembly workflow (refs.bib) for traceability and post-hoc review.

1.title: Introduction
1.summary: Motivate the challenge of reliable long-form scientific writing with large language models, state the research question—how does graph-guided sectioning affect coherence and citation quality?—and give a high-level overview of the graph-guided prompting workflow and conservative claim policy (always cite sources).

2.title: Related Work
2.summary: Review prior approaches to long-form generation, structured prompting, citation-aware generation, and document planning. Contrast linear prompting baselines and citation verification techniques, emphasizing gaps addressed by a graph-aware approach.

3.title: Methods
3.summary: Detail the graph construction (section graph and dependencies), the JSON schema for section outputs, evidence retrieval and ranking, evidence-aware prompt templates, leaf-first generation and assembly rules, and the LaTeX + refs.bib assembly process. Include conservative validation checks and failure modes.

4.title: Experiments
4.summary: Describe experimental setup: two topical domains, baseline linear prompting comparator, datasets (internal notes and a small curated PDF set if available), and evaluation protocol. Specify metrics: citation coverage, hallucination rate (unsupported assertions), and reviewer score.

5.title: Results
5.summary: Report quantitative outcomes on citation coverage, hallucination rates, and reviewer scores, with qualitative examples illustrating error modes and successful evidence integration. Emphasize conservative interpretation of improvements and per-topic variability.

6.title: Discussion
6.summary: Analyze why graph-guided scheduling affects coherence and citation placement, limitations (dataset scale, domain transfer, reliance on retrieval quality), and implications for auditability and reproducibility. Propose mitigations and future extensions.

7.title: Conclusion
7.summary: Summarize contributions and findings, restate emphasis on conservative claims and mandatory citations, and outline next steps for larger-scale evaluation and community-shared datasets and tools.

3-1.title: Section graph construction and scheduling
3-1.summary: Describe construction of the document section graph, node and edge semantics (section dependencies, prerequisite relations), graph serialization, and the leaf-first scheduling algorithm used to order section generation.

3-2.title: JSON schema for section outputs
3-2.summary: Specify the strict JSON schema for each generated section (fields, types, required citation/evidence fields, machine-checkable constraints), validation procedure, and how JSON outputs facilitate edits and audits.

3-3.title: Evidence retrieval, ranking, and injection protocol
3-3.summary: Detail the retrieval sources and indexing, query formulation, ranking/scoring of candidate evidence, selection thresholds, and the protocol for injecting ranked evidence into section prompts.

3-4.title: Evidence-aware prompt templates and JSON-constrained generation
3-4.summary: Present the prompt template families that enforce citation-first writing, instruct JSON-constrained outputs, include evidence citation anchors, and describe iterative generation/validation loops for a single section.

3-5.title: Assembly into LaTeX + refs.bib, validation checks, and failure modes
3-5.summary: Explain rules for assembling JSON sections into a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib, conservative validation checks (citation coverage, unsupported-claim detection), logging, and documented failure modes and remediation steps.

4-1.title: Experimental setup and datasets
4-1.summary: Describe the overall experimental design: the two topical domains used for evaluation, how internal notes and the small curated PDF set are incorporated, data splits or sampling procedures, and implementation details required to reproduce the experiments (model versions, prompting pipeline, and compute/provider notes). Emphasize constraints relevant to reproducibility and evidence injection per section.

4-2.title: Baselines, metrics, and evaluation protocol
4-2.summary: Specify the baseline linear prompting comparator, exact evaluation metrics (citation coverage, hallucination rate/unsupported assertions, and reviewer-style scoring), annotation or adjudication procedures for unsupported assertions, and the statistical or qualitative analysis plan used to compare methods.

6-1.title: Graph-guided scheduling: effects on coherence and citation placement
6-1.summary: Analyze how leaf-first, dependency-aware ordering influences local and global coherence, rhetorical flow between sections, and the timing/location of evidence citations; identify scenarios where graph structure most improves citation clustering or clarity and where it can introduce disconnects between sections.

6-2.title: Limitations, failure modes, and practical mitigations
6-2.summary: Discuss limitations such as small dataset scale, domain-transfer risks, and dependence on retrieval quality; enumerate practical mitigations (data augmentation, retrieval re-ranking, human-in-the-loop checks) and short-term validation strategies to detect and reduce unsupported assertions.

6-3.title: Implications for auditability, reproducibility, and future work
6-3.summary: Describe how JSON-constrained outputs and explicit evidence injection improve auditability and reproducibility; propose extensions (richer graph encodings, multi-stage retrieval, evaluation on larger/other domains) and outline next steps for tooling and evaluation to facilitate community adoption.
